read.glossary.0.word.note: "Collective learning" is "pembelajaran kolektif". Accurate but abstract for young readers; "belajar bersama" is easier but loses the idea of knowledge building up over generations.

read.glossary.3.word.note: "Hearth" is "tungku". A tungku is often a cooking stove of stones; I used it for both "hearth" and "fireplaces" in section 2 so learners meet one word. "Perapian" is the alternative.

read.sections.1.text.note: "cut a neat pattern into a piece of red rock" is "mengukir pola yang rapi pada sepotong batu merah"; kept "Gua Blombos" as the place name.
read.sections.1.text.back: Early humans did not leave any written records, so how can we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, hearths and artwork. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burnt seeds/grains inside a hearth can show what people cooked. Artwork shows that people used marks and symbols. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone carved a neat pattern on a piece of red stone about 75,000 years ago. However, one object can rarely prove the whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.
read.sections.1.text.source: Early humans did not leave any written records, so how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things that people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, fireplaces and art. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked. Art shows that people used signs and symbols. In Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone cut a neat pattern into a piece of red rock about 75,000 years ago. However, one object rarely proves a whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: "A worn tool" became "Alat yang sudah lama dipakai" (a tool used for a long time), because "aus" may be hard for slow readers.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Early humans did not write. So, how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things people left behind. Tools, bones and artwork are clues. A tool that has been used for a long time shows how people used it. Burnt seeds in a hearth show what people cooked. In South Africa, people scratched lines on red stone. That was about 75,000 years ago. But one object does not tell everything. So, archaeologists look at many finds.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Early humans did not write. So how do we learn about them? An archaeologist studies things that people left behind. Tools, bones and art are all clues. read.sections.0.text.back: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are very good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, improve it, then teach it to someone else. In this way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, someone might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Other people copy that idea, change it a little, then pass it on, so the idea is not lost when one person stops using it.
read.sections.0.text.source: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, improve it and then teach it to others. In this way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little and pass it on, so it is not lost when one person stops using it.

A good idea does not stop at one person.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Moving and adapting in new places
read.sections.2.heading.source: Moving and adapting to new places

read.sections.2.text.back: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over thousands of years, groups of humans slowly spread to Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long journey. It happened little by little, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, then made new tools and clothes. To get to Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have made boats. A tool may look simple, but making it takes planning, skill and teaching.
read.sections.2.text.source: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over many thousands of years, groups slowly spread into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long trip. It happened a little at a time, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, and they made new tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. A tool may look simple, but making it took planning, skill and teaching.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: According to scientists, humans like us first lived in Africa. That was about 300,000 years ago. Slowly, groups of humans spread to other parts of the world. This took thousands of years. It did not happen in one journey. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and weather. To get to Australia, they crossed the sea by boat. A tool may look simple. But making it takes skill and has to be taught.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Scientists say our kind of human first lived in Africa. That was about 300,000 years ago. Slowly, groups spread to other parts of the world. This took many thousands of years. It did not happen in one trip. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and weather. To reach Australia, they crossed the sea in boats. A tool may look simple. But making it took skill and teaching.

write.example.back: These clues indicate that early humans learned skills from each other. Clue 4 shows tools with the same shape at sites far apart. This may mean people copied a good design and taught it to others. Another clue is the hearth with layers of ash. People may have used the same fire place many times and shared what they knew about fire and food. Together, these clues indicate collective learning. But these clues cannot tell us what words people used or who made the first tool.

watch.summary.back: This video explains collective learning. Humans can use language to share ideas in great detail. So one person does not have to learn everything alone. Each generation can learn what older people know, then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways of finding food, making tools, using fire and building shelters. This helped groups of humans adapt in many different places, from hot areas to cold areas. We cannot hear what early humans said. But tools slowly became better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning does not make every group the same. Each community uses what it knows in its own way, suited to its place.

Each generation can learn what older people knew and then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelter. This helped groups adapt to many different places, from hot lands to cold ones. We cannot hear what early people said. But tools slowly got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning did not make every group the same. Each community used what it knew in its own way, to fit its own place.
